name: Noisy Dish
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, built to Hall of Femme's
brief. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's and
is stated in the same two references: the frame fetch, the vertical
output, the transcription, the rewrite, and how the caption is set.
Where it parts company with its neighbours is not the type at all, it
is the PICTURE. Every other channel under this heading delivers the
still edge to edge and puts a card of type on it. This one delivers
the still as a card of its own, lying on a ground the channel paints
- see `photo` below - and then sets the caption in nothing but white
letters, because the picture is now carrying all the graphic the frame
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of a sibling, for
the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that gets
dropped in. The prose below points at hall-of-femme wherever the
reasoning is the same and states its own where this pack decides
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into report.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a pack
that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
_comment_photo: The still, resized and laid on a painted ground. This is the whole of
what makes the channel look like itself, and the three parts of it are
one composition rather than three effects - see `photo` in
js/channels.js for what each key means and why the geometry is stated
the way it is.
85% of the frame, centred. Both dimensions by the same fraction, which
is the only scaling that leaves the picture the picture: the still
arrives already cut to 540x960 (see snapchat-capture), so 0.85 is
459x816 and the crop the backend chose survives it intact. What the
margin is for is the ground: 41px of it down each side and 72px top
and bottom, which is a band of the gradient rather than a field of it
- enough to read as the frame's colour and as a deliberate edge, and
not so much that the still stops being the thing on screen.
13px of corner radius, the same 13 the caption cards elsewhere under
this heading are rounded by (see snapchat-caption). Same reason, too:
a square-cornered picture inset on a coloured ground reads as a
letterbox, something the player did, and a rounded one reads as a
graphic somebody made.
The backdrop runs on the diagonal: crimson in the bottom-left corner,
amber in the top-right. [0,1] to [1,0] is that corner to that corner,
measured across the canvas - the ramp is stated as the two ends of the
line it travels along and nothing about the size of what it crosses,
so it is the same statement whatever the card is sized to.
A diagonal rather than a fall down the frame, and it is what makes the
margin worth having at 85%: a band this narrow crossed by a top-to-
bottom ramp is two flat stripes, one down each side, because the sides
are where nearly all of it is and each side is a single height. Run
corner to corner, every edge of that band travels through the whole
ramp instead, and the frame reads as one field of colour with a
picture lying on it.
The tint is one colour and it is the join between the two halves of
the composition: a brick that is what the crimson and the amber have
in common, laid over the picture so the card looks lit by the ground
it is lying on instead of pasted onto it. Full strength along the
bottom edge of the card and gone by the top, which is the direction
every shade in this app is thrown in (see `scrim`) and the one that
puts the deepest colour where the picture meets the caption. It is a
treatment OF the photograph and is clipped to it, corners included -
that is what `tint` is for and what separates it from a scrim, which
would run out across the ground.
To wash the whole picture evenly instead, give both stops the same
alpha; the direction and the fade are these two stops and nothing
else.
_comment_title: Bebas Neue, white, and nothing else. Every other decision about how a
caption is set under this heading - the size, where the lines break,
the capitals, where the block stands, that the user can drag it off a
face - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
Bebas has no lower case of its own, so the preset's capitals are the
face's own answer rather than a transformation laid over it (see
content/faces/bebas-neue.json).
At the preset's 120px bottom margin the block sits inside the card,
48px up from its bottom edge, and grows upward from there however
long the caption runs. That is the deepest part of the tint, which is
what makes a card of its own unnecessary: the letters are on the one
band of the picture this channel has already painted a known colour,
rather than on an unknown photograph - which is the whole of the
argument the preset makes for a card in the first place.
It is a margin the card can lose, though, and that is worth knowing
before either number is touched. The block is measured off the FRAME
and not off the card, so shrinking the picture moves the card's foot
up while the type stays where it is: at 0.70 the same caption crossed
the bottom edge and stood half in the ground. Nothing breaks when it
does - the amber below is the palest thing in the frame and the type
carries an opaque black shadow - but the two numbers are related and
the relation is not in either of them.

_comment_color: Pure white, on every frame, with no palette offered beside it.
That is a brand decision rather than a missing feature: the
colour in this channel is the ground and the tint, and a second
colour in the type would be a third thing competing with them.
Hall of Femme hands two of its colours to the user because the
PAIRING of card and letters is what that show is; here there is
no card, so there is no pairing to offer.
_comment_shadow: Absolute black, at the app's own shadow geometry, and it is doing
real work rather than decorating. The preset drops the shadow
because its caption sits on a solid card in a colour somebody
picked; this one has no card and stands on the amber foot of the
gradient, so white letters need something under them again.
Opaque rather than the 0.8 black everywhere else in this app: the
ground it has to hold the type against is a bright warm colour of
known contrast, not an unknown photograph, and against amber a
translucent shadow reads as a muddy edge instead of as a shadow.
_comment_panel: None. The preset's card is exactly what this channel does not
have: the still has already been shrunk to make room for a
coloured ground, and a slab of a third colour laid over that
ground would be a background in front of a background.
Stated as null rather than left out, because the preset states
one and a pack that says nothing inherits it whole.
_comment_highlight: None either, and it follows from the two decisions above rather
than being a decision of its own. A highlight under this heading
is one of three things: another colour, another cut of the face,
or a box. The type here is always pure white, so a colour is out;
Bebas Neue ships as a single cut, so a second weight is out; and
a box is a background, which is the one thing this channel does
The word buttons in the panel stay where they are and go dead,
with a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderWordButtons) - a live button that produced no
visible change would read as the app ignoring the click.
